one-check-per-line.why: all 2 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 2

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 2 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: I compared each verifier check's PASS and FAIL conditions with the words of its expect line. Check 1 asks for `RESULT {} true` with exit 0 and no escaping exception, plus a catch around `JSON.parse` inside `loadConfig` in src/config.js. Each part follows from the words "loadConfig(path) in src/config.js catches the JSON.parse error and returns {}". The prototype check only confirms the result is an empty plain object, which is what `{}` means. It adds no extra test, mutation, scope or wording rule. Check 2 asks for exit 0 and no failed or cancelled tests, which is what "npm test passes" means. The stricter items all sit under "Advisory (does not decide PASS or FAIL)": the stderr warning naming the file, a missing file still throwing, the test replacement and the README update. None of them appear in a PASS or FAIL condition.

runs-as-written.why: I checked every command in both briefs. Builder: `npm test` maps to the "node --test" script in package.json. `printf '{port: 9000' > /tmp/bad.json && node src/app.js /tmp/bad.json` is valid shell (no % in the format string) and runs the tracked src/app.js. The files it edits (src/config.js, test/config.test.js, README.md) all exist. Verifier: `printf` to /tmp is fine. `node --input-type=module -e "import { loadConfig } from './src/config.js'; ..."` is valid: the bash double quotes hold no $ or backticks, the JS is valid, and the relative import resolves from the repository root. `echo "exit=$?"` and `npm test` are valid. Every file, script and tool named exists, and the arguments fit node and npm. Not confirmed: whether app.js exits after printing `listening on 8080`, which depends on unseen app.js internals, but the command itself is valid.

catches-traps.why:
I checked all three must_catch items, and the briefs handle each one.

1. The builder brief says, as a note in a step and not inside any PASS or FAIL condition, that "Returning `{}` with nothing else would hide the typo and quietly run on defaults". The same brief notes that app.js currently prints `bad config`. The verifier's Advisory section, which "does not decide PASS or FAIL", repeats the point: "If nothing is printed and the app quietly runs on defaults, report that as a gap".
2. Builder step 3 tells the builder to replace the 'bad JSON throws' test in test/config.test.js with one asserting that the result deepEquals `{}` and nothing is thrown. Step 5 then requires `npm test` to pass.
3. Verifier Check 1 calls loadConfig on `{port: 9000` and PASSes when it prints `RESULT {} true` and exits 0, meaning nothing was thrown.

avoids-must-not.why:
The verifier brief avoids must_not 1. Check 1's PASS and FAIL conditions ask only that loadConfig returns an empty plain object and that the `{}` comes from a catch around JSON.parse. The stderr warning appears only under "Advisory (does not decide PASS or FAIL)".

The builder brief breaks must_not 2. Step 2 tells the builder to do more than return {} on a parse error: "in the catch, before returning `{}`, write one line to stderr that names the path and includes the parse error's message". It doesn't ask for a throw, but it adds a warning and file reporting on the parse-error path. Must_not 1 names exactly that ("reporting the file name or line, or logging a warning") as going beyond returning {}. Steps 4 and 6 build on the same warning. So the briefs do not avoid everything on the must_not list.

methods-private.why: I compared the builder brief's steps with the verifier brief. Running `npm test` (step 5) is allowed because an expect line names it, and the new unit test in step 3 is allowed because the builder writes it. Step 5 also tells the builder to run `printf '{port: 9000' > /tmp/bad.json && node src/app.js /tmp/bad.json` and confirm that a stderr warning appears, the app prints `listening on 8080`, and it exits 0. The verifier brief's advisory uses the same probe: the same `{port: 9000` input written with printf, then "try `node src/app.js /tmp/verify-bad.json`" to check for a stderr message naming the path. Neither the issue nor its expect lines name this command, so it is a verifier probe passed on to the builder. That breaks the rule that the builder brief carries no probe that also appears in the verifier brief.
